questions.question: A night light uses an LED (constant resistance 340 ohm) and a resistor R = 860 ohm. The light goes out when the LED p.d. falls to 1.4 V, and the time should be as close to 10 minutes as possible but not less. Choose the capacitance from 0.50, 0.51, 0.54, 0.58 and 0.60 F.
steps: The capacitor discharges through R and the LED in series: R_total = 860 + 340 = 1200 ohm.
The LED goes out when its p.d. is 1.4 V. The p.d. divides in the ratio of resistances, so the capacitor p.d. is then V = 1.4 x 1200 / 340 = 4.94 V.
Discharge: V = V0 e^(-t/RC) with V0 = 12 V, so t = RC ln(12 / 4.94) = 1200 C x 0.887 = 1065 C seconds.
Need t >= 600 s, so C >= 600 / 1065 = 0.56 F. The smallest available value not below this is 0.58 F (t = 618 s, about 10.3 min); 0.54 F gives only 575 s, which is too short.

questions.question: The LED's resistance is not constant. Using its current against p.d. graph, explain how this behaviour affects the time for the light intensity to decrease to zero.
questions.answer: The time for the light to go out is longer than the student calculated, because the LED resistance rises as the p.d. falls.
steps: Below about 1.4 V the LED current is almost zero, so the LED resistance becomes very large (the graph is flat), and as the capacitor p.d. falls the LED resistance increases.

A larger resistance means a larger time constant RC, so the capacitor discharges more and more slowly and the current (and light intensity) decreases more slowly than the constant-resistance model predicts.

With a constant 340 ohm LED the light stopped when the capacitor was at about 4.9 V, but with the real LED the current only reaches zero when the capacitor p.d. has fallen to about 1.4 V, so the light takes longer to decrease to zero than the student's calculation of about 10 minutes.

questions.question: A student says the function of a capacitor in the circuit is to store electric charge. Explain why this is not a complete description of its function.
questions.answer: A capacitor also stores energy and releases it over time; with the resistor it controls the rate at which the p.d. and current decay, through the time constant RC.
steps: A charged capacitor stores energy, E = 0.5 Q V = 0.5 C V^2, not just charge.
When the supply is removed, the stored energy is released as a current through the resistor.
The rate of release is set by the time constant RC, so the p.d. decays gradually rather than instantly.
This controlled release is what gives the night light its slow fade, so the complete function is to store and release energy at a controlled rate.

questions.question: A capacitor of capacitance C with p.d. V stores charge Q. It is replaced by two capacitors of capacitance 2C in parallel. Select the total charge stored from the options.
questions.answer: D: 4Q
steps: Original charge Q = CV.
Capacitors in parallel add: 2C + 2C = 4C, with the same p.d. V across them.
Total charge = 4C x V = 4Q (option D).

questions.question: A battery of e.m.f. V charges an initially uncharged capacitor, transferring charge Q with final p.d. V. Select the row giving the work done by the battery and the energy stored.
questions.answer: C: work done by the battery = QV; energy stored = QV/2
steps: The battery moves charge Q through its e.m.f. V, so it does work W = QV.
The energy stored in the capacitor is the area under the V-Q graph: E = QV/2.
The other half of the battery's energy, QV/2, is dissipated as heat in the circuit resistance, so the row is C.

questions.question: Two capacitors, each of capacitance 32 uF, are connected to a 6.0 V battery as shown. Calculate the total charge stored.
steps: The diagram shows the two capacitors in parallel across the 6.0 V battery, so the capacitances add: C = 32 + 32 = 64 microfarad.

questions.question: Calculate the total energy stored by the two 32 uF capacitors connected to the 6.0 V battery as shown.
steps: The capacitors are in parallel, so total C = 64 x 10^-6 F, with 6.0 V across them.

questions.question: Add to the diagram a suitable circuit for charging and discharging the capacitor through the resistor while measuring the p.d. across the capacitor.
questions.answer: Battery (6.0 V) and a two-way switch connecting the capacitor-resistor series branch to the battery (charging) or round a closed loop (discharging), with a voltmeter in parallel with the capacitor.
steps: Add the 6.0 V battery in series with a two-way switch, so that in position 1 the battery is connected to the series resistor and capacitor and the capacitor charges through the resistor.
In position 2 the capacitor and resistor are connected to each other only, giving a closed loop so that the capacitor discharges through the resistor.
Connect a voltmeter directly across the capacitor (in parallel with it, not across the resistor) to record the capacitor p.d. during charging and discharging.

questions.question: On the same axes as the capacitor p.d. against time graph, sketch how the p.d. across the resistor varies with time during charging.
questions.answer: An exponential decay from 6.0 V at t = 0 towards 0 V, the mirror image of the capacitor curve in the 3.0 V line; it crosses the capacitor curve at 3.0 V at about 3.3 s.
steps: The cell p.d. is shared between the capacitor and resistor: V_R = 6.0 - V_C.
At t = 0 the capacitor p.d. is zero so V_R = 6.0 V; V_R falls with a decreasing gradient and approaches 0 V as t increases (V_R = 6.0 e^(-t/RC), about 2.2 V at t = RC = 4.8 s).
The two curves cross at 3.0 V (V_C = V_R = V0 / 2) at t = RC ln 2, about 3.3 s.

questions.question: Show that the p.d. V across the capacitor during charging is V = V0 - V0 e^(-t/RC), where V0 is the e.m.f., R the resistance and C the capacitance.
steps: Kirchhoff's voltage law: V0 = I R + q / C, where q / C is the p.d. across the capacitor.
The current is I = dq / dt, so V0 = R dq/dt + q / C.
Rearranging: dq/dt = (C V0 - q) / (RC), which has solution q = C V0 (1 - e^(-t/RC)).
The capacitor p.d. is V = q / C = V0 (1 - e^(-t/RC)) = V0 - V0 e^(-t/RC).

questions.question: The student recorded the p.d. across the capacitor and the resistance (330 kohm) during charging. From the list of 10, 15, 47, 100 and 150 uF capacitors, deduce the capacitance used.
questions.answer: 15 microfarad
steps: The time constant is the time for the capacitor p.d. to reach 63 percent of 6.0 V, that is 3.8 V. From the graph this is at t of about 4.8 s, so RC = 4.8 s.
C = (time constant) / R = 4.8 / 330 000 = 1.5 x 10^-5 F = 15 microfarad.

Check with another point: for 15 microfarad RC = 4.95 s and V at 10 s = 6.0(1 - e^(-10/4.95)) = 5.2 V, in agreement with the graph; 10 microfarad (RC = 3.3 s) or 47 microfarad (RC = 15.5 s) would not fit.

questions.question: Calculate the charge on the fully charged capacitor, using the capacitance found in part (iii).
steps: Fully charged, the capacitor p.d. equals the e.m.f. of the battery, 6.0 V.

questions.question: Calculate the energy stored by the fully charged capacitor, using the capacitance found in part (iii).
An uncharged capacitor, resistor, switch and cell are connected. Select the graphs showing how the charge on the capacitor and the p.d. across the resistor vary with time after the switch is closed.
questions.answer: C: charge rises with time (levelling off), p.d. across the resistor falls with time
steps: When the switch is closed the uncharged capacitor charges up, so the charge on it increases from zero towards a maximum with a decreasing gradient.
The cell p.d. is shared by the resistor and capacitor: V_R = V0 - V_C. As V_C rises the p.d. across the resistor falls exponentially from V0 towards zero (the current falls).
Only graph pair C shows charge rising and the resistor p.d. falling.

questions.question: A charged capacitor discharges through a resistor of resistance R. A graph of ln(current) against time has gradient g. Select the expression giving the capacitance.
questions.answer: B: C = -1 / (gradient x R)
steps: During discharge I = I0 e^(-t/RC), so ln I = ln I0 - t/(RC).
A graph of ln I against t is a straight line with gradient = -1/(RC).
Rearranging, RC = -1/gradient, so C = -1 / (gradient x R) (option B).

questions.question: Explain how the circuit can maintain power to the electronic controller when the switch (the contact with the rails) is opened for a short time.
questions.answer: While the switch is closed the capacitor is charged; when it opens, the capacitor discharges through the resistor and supplies the controller, so the p.d. falls only slowly.
steps: While the switch is closed, the capacitor charges and stores energy.
When the switch opens, the capacitor becomes the source of power for the controller.
It discharges through the resistor, so the p.d. across the controller falls gradually rather than dropping to zero at once.
The discharge time is set by the time constant RC, so a large capacitance keeps the controller powered for a short break in contact.

questions.question: With the switch opened, the capacitor (47 mF) discharges through a 470 ohm resistor, the controller having infinite resistance. Calculate the time for the capacitor p.d. to fall to 4.0 V.
steps: With the switch closed the capacitor is connected directly across the 12 V battery, so it is charged to V0 = 12 V when the switch opens.
The capacitor then discharges through the 470 ohm resistor: RC = 470 x 47 x 10^-3 = 22.1 s.

questions.question: The switch is closed at t = 0 and opened at t = 20 s. Sketch a graph of the current through the resistor against time.
questions.answer: A constant current of about 25.5 mA from t = 0 to 20 s, then an exponential decay from 25.5 mA at t = 20 s (time constant 22 s), reaching about 10 mA at t = 40 s.
steps: With the switch closed, the 470 ohm resistor is connected directly across the 12 V battery, so I = 12 / 470 = 25.5 mA, constant from t = 0 to t = 20 s (a horizontal line).

The capacitor is charged to 12 V, so when the switch opens at t = 20 s the current in the resistor is still 25.5 mA, and then decays exponentially as the capacitor discharges (same direction, so it stays positive).
The decay is I = 25.5 e^(-(t-20)/22.1) mA with time constant RC = 22.1 s, so the current has fallen to 37 percent (9.4 mA) at t = 42 s and is about 10 mA at t = 40 s.

questions.question: The graph shows charge Q against p.d. V for a capacitor. Select the expression giving the energy stored when V is 12 V.
steps: The energy stored is the area under the Q-V graph, a triangle: E = 1/2 Q V.
At 12 V the charge is 550 nC = 550 x 10^-9 C, so E = (550 x 10^-9 x 12) / 2 = 3.3 x 10^-6 J (option D).
A and B are not energies, and C has not converted nC to C.

questions.question: The capacitor in the defibrillator is discharged, then the switch is moved to S1 at t = 0. Complete the graph to show how the current varies with time until the capacitor is fully charged.
questions.answer: An exponential decay curve starting at 7.7 x 10^-2 A (77 mA) at t = 0 and falling towards zero (about 2.8 x 10^-2 A at t = 2.2 s).
steps: At t = 0 the capacitor is uncharged, so the whole 5000 V is across the 65 kohm resistor: I0 = 5000 / 65 000 = 0.077 A.
As the capacitor charges, its p.d. rises and the p.d. across the resistor falls, so the current falls exponentially, with a decreasing gradient, towards zero when the capacitor is fully charged.
Time constant RC = 65 000 x 34 x 10^-6 = 2.2 s: the current falls to 37 percent (0.028 A) at t = 2.2 s, and is about zero by about 10 s.

questions.question: The defibrillator must deliver a discharge current of at least 30 A for 2.0 ms through a body resistance of 150 ohm. Deduce whether the design meets this requirement.
questions.answer: No: the current starts at 33 A but falls below 30 A after about 0.54 ms, so it is not at least 30 A for 2.0 ms.
steps: The fully charged capacitor has p.d. 5000 V (the supply), so the initial discharge current through the body is I0 = V/R = 5000 / 150 = 33 A.
Time constant = RC = 150 x 34 x 10^-6 = 5.1 x 10^-3 s = 5.1 ms.
I = I0 e^(-t/RC): after 2.0 ms I = 33.3 x e^(-2.0/5.1) = 22.5 A, which is less than 30 A.
The current drops to 30 A at t = RC ln(33.3/30) = 5.1 x 0.105 = 0.54 ms, so the design does not meet the requirement (30 A for 2.0 ms).

questions.question: Sketch a graph of the p.d. VC across the capacitor against time after the switch is closed, marking the time constant T on the time axis.
questions.answer: An exponential rise from 0 at t = 0, with decreasing gradient, levelling off at 5 V; at t = T the p.d. is about 3.2 V (63 percent of 5 V).
steps: At t = 0 the capacitor is uncharged, so V_C = 0.
V_C = 5(1 - e^(-t/RC)) rises steeply at first then flattens, approaching the supply p.d. of 5 V (asymptote).
At the time constant t = T = RC, V_C = 0.63 x 5 = 3.2 V; mark this point on the curve above T.

questions.question: Explain how the p.d. VR across the resistor varies with time after the switch is closed.
questions.answer: VR starts at the full supply p.d. and falls exponentially to zero as the capacitor charges, because VR = V0 - VC.
steps: Just after the switch closes, the capacitor is uncharged so its p.d. is zero.
By Kirchhoff's voltage law the whole supply p.d. appears across the resistor at t = 0.
As the capacitor charges, VC rises, so VR = V0 - VC falls.
VR decreases exponentially to zero, with the time constant RC controlling the rate.

questions.question: Show that the p.d. VC across the capacitor is given by VC = V0 (1 - e^(-t/RC)), where R is the resistance and C the capacitance. The integrated circuit has infinite resistance.
steps: Infinite resistance of the integrated circuit means no current flows through it, so the same current flows through R and C.
Kirchhoff: V0 = I R + q / C with I = dq / dt, giving dq/dt = (C V0 - q) / (RC).
Solving with q = 0 at t = 0 gives q = C V0 (1 - e^(-t/RC)).
So VC = q / C = V0 (1 - e^(-t/RC)).

questions.question: The input to an integrated circuit should be 3.3 V at 3.5 s after the switch is closed, with R = 68 kohm. Choose a capacitor from 4.7, 10, 15, 47 and 150 uF.
questions.answer: 47 microfarad
steps: C = 3.24 / (68 x 10^3) = 4.8 x 10^-5 F = 48 microfarad, so the 47 microfarad capacitor should be used (it gives V_C = 3.33 V).

questions.question: Determine whether the initial value of current on the graph is consistent with the values stated on the circuit diagram.
questions.answer: Yes, consistent: I0 = 5.0 / 33 000 = 1.5 x 10^-4 A = 0.15 mA, which matches the 0.15 mA at t = 0 on the graph.
steps: At t = 0 the capacitor is uncharged, so the whole 5.0 V is across the 33 kohm resistor.
The graph starts at 0.15 mA, so the initial current is consistent with the circuit values.

questions.question: Explain how the current on ammeter A2 would vary over the same time interval.
questions.answer: The reading on A2 is the same as on A1 at all times: it starts at 0.15 mA and falls exponentially to zero.
steps: A1 and A2 are in series in the same loop, so the same current flows through both at any instant.

Charge flows onto one plate and off the other plate of the capacitor at the same rate (no current passes through the dielectric), so A2 shows the same exponentially decaying current as A1, from 0.15 mA to about zero over 30 s.

questions.question: Using the current-time graph and the circuit values, determine the capacitance of the capacitor.
questions.answer: C = 2.2 x 10^-4 F (about 220 microfarad)
steps: The current decays as I = I0 e^(-t/RC). The time constant RC is the time for the current to fall to I0/e = 0.15/2.72 = 0.055 mA, which the graph gives at t of about 7 s.
Check: at t = 10 s the graph shows about 0.037 mA, and 0.15 e^(-10/7.1) = 0.037 mA, so RC = 7 s.

questions.question: Determine the charge stored on the capacitor after 30 s.
steps: After 30 s (about 4 time constants) the current has fallen to about zero, so the capacitor is almost fully charged to the 5.0 V supply p.d.
Check: the area under the I-t graph is about I0 x RC = 0.15 x 10^-3 x 7.1 = 1.1 x 10^-3 C.

questions.question: Determine the maximum energy stored by the capacitor.
steps: The maximum energy is stored when the capacitor is fully charged to 5.0 V.

questions.question: Which of the following units is equivalent to the farad? A: C V^-1; B: J V^-1; C: s^-1; D: s J^-1.
questions.answer: A: C V^-1 (coulomb per volt).
steps: Capacitance is defined as C = Q / V.
Charge is measured in coulombs and potential difference in volts.
So the farad is equivalent to C V^-1, which is option A.

questions.question: When the p.d. across a capacitor is V, the energy stored is W. Select the energy stored when the p.d. is 2V.
questions.answer: D: 4W.
steps: Energy stored by a capacitor is W = 0.5 C V^2, which depends on V squared.
With the p.d. doubled, the energy becomes 0.5 C (2V)^2 = 4 x (0.5 C V^2) = 4W.
So the answer is option D, 4W.

questions.question: A capacitor discharges through a resistor with time constant 5 s. Select the time for the charge on the plates to halve.
questions.answer: D: 5 ln2 s (about 3.5 s).
steps: Charge decays as Q = Q0 e^(-t/RC) = Q0 e^(-t/5).
Halving the charge requires e^(-t/5) = 0.5.
Taking logarithms gives t / 5 = ln 2, so t = 5 ln2 s, which is option D.

questions.question: A light conducting sphere of radius r = 3.5 cm is charged by touching one of two plates separated by d = 5.0 cm with a potential difference of 4500 V. The sphere has capacitance C = 4 pi epsilon0 r. Calculate the electrostatic force on the sphere.
questions.answer: Electrostatic force = 1.6 x 10^-3 N.
steps: Capacitance of the sphere C = 4 pi epsilon0 r = 1.11 x 10^-10 x 0.035 = 3.89 x 10^-12 F.
On touching the 4500 V plate the sphere takes the plate potential, so Q = C V = 3.89 x 10^-12 x 4500 = 1.75 x 10^-8 C.
The field between the plates is E = V / d = 4500 / 0.050 = 9.0 x 10^4 V m^-1.
The electrostatic force on the sphere is F = Q E = 1.75 x 10^-8 x 9.0 x 10^4 = 1.6 x 10^-3 N.

questions.question: After charging, the conducting sphere oscillates between the two plates, touching each alternately. Explain why it oscillates.
questions.answer: On touching a plate the sphere takes that plate's charge, is then repelled by it and attracted to the opposite plate, where it loses charge and repeats the cycle.
steps: The sphere touches the positive plate, gains positive charge, and is repelled from that plate.
The sphere is then attracted to the negative plate across the gap.
On contact with the negative plate, it gains negative charge (neutralising its positive charge), so it is repelled back.
The sequence of attraction, contact and repulsion repeats, so the sphere oscillates between the plates.

questions.question: In Franklin's version, one bell is earthed and the other is connected to a positively charged lightning conductor. The sphere is initially uncharged. Explain why the sphere starts to move between the bells.
questions.answer: The positive bell induces a negative charge on the near side of the uncharged sphere, so it is attracted; on contact it becomes positive and is then repelled to the earthed bell, and the cycle repeats.
steps: The positively charged bell polarises the uncharged sphere, inducing negative charge on its near side.
The sphere is attracted towards the positive bell and touches it.
Charge is transferred, the sphere becomes positive, and it is repelled towards the earthed bell.
On reaching the earthed bell it discharges and the cycle repeats, so the sphere moves between the bells.

questions.question: The capacitor is labelled 470 uF with a tolerance of 10 percent. Using the discharge graph through 150 kohm, evaluate whether the capacitance is within the stated tolerance.
questions.answer: C = about 5.0 x 10^-4 F (500 microfarad), which is 6 percent above 470 microfarad, so it is within the +/-10 percent tolerance.
steps: During discharge V = V0 e^(-t/RC). V0 = 12 V at t = 0, and the time constant RC is the time for V to fall to V0/e = 12/2.72 = 4.4 V, which the graph gives at t = 75 s.
Check with another point: V = 3.2 V at t = 100 s gives RC = 100 / ln(12/3.2) = 76 s.

The tolerance range is 470 +/- 10 percent = 423 to 517 microfarad. 500 microfarad is inside this range (6 percent above the marked value), so the capacitor is within the stated tolerance (though in the upper part of it).

questions.question: An ultracapacitor of capacitance 47 F can store a maximum charge of 56 C. It is suggested it can store 1000 times the energy of a 470 uF capacitor at 12 V. Assess the validity of this suggestion.
questions.answer: Valid: the ultracapacitor can store up to about 33 J, while a 470 uF capacitor at 12 V stores about 0.034 J, a ratio of about 990, which is close to 1000.
steps: Energy stored by the 470 uF capacitor at 12 V: W = 0.5 C V^2 = 0.5 x 470 x 10^-6 x 12^2 = 0.0338 J.
Maximum energy stored by the ultracapacitor: W = Q^2 / (2C) = 56^2 / (2 x 47) = 33.4 J.
Ratio = 33.4 / 0.0338 = 990, which is about 1000.
So the suggestion is valid: the ultracapacitor stores about 1000 times as much energy (the 12 V applies only to the 470 uF capacitor).

questions.question: There is a p.d. of 6 V across a 220 uF capacitor. Select the expression giving the charge stored.
steps: Charge stored Q = CV.
C = 220 microfarad = 2.2 x 10^-4 F and V = 6 V, so Q = 2.2 x 10^-4 x 6 = 1.3 x 10^-3 C (option B).
Option A includes a factor 1/2 (that would be the energy), and C and D divide by V, which is wrong.

questions.question: The capacitor is marked 22 uF and is charged through a 240 kohm resistor while the current is measured. Using the graph of current against time, show that the marked value is correct.
questions.answer: C = 2.2 x 10^-5 F (22 microfarad), matching the marked value.
steps: While charging the current is I = I0 e^(-t/RC), so ln I = ln I0 - t/(RC): the ln I against t graph is a straight line of gradient -1/(RC).
C = 5.3 / R = 5.3 / 240 000 = 2.2 x 10^-5 F = 22 microfarad, which agrees with the value marked on the capacitor.

questions.question: Sphere B rises to a maximum height h = 1.1 cm after the collision. Calculate its maximum speed immediately after the collision.
questions.answer: Maximum speed = 0.46 m s^-1.
steps: After the collision, sphere B rises to height h, so all its kinetic energy becomes gravitational potential energy at the top.
0.5 m v^2 = m g h, so v = sqrt(2 g h).

questions.question: During contact the capacitor (22 uF) discharges through a circuit of resistance 49 ohm, with p.d. falling from 6.18 V to 5.43 V. Calculate the time the spheres were in contact.
questions.answer: Time in contact = 1.4 x 10^-4 s (0.14 ms).
steps: Discharge law: V = V0 e^(-t/RC), so t = RC ln(V0 / V).

questions.question: The student states the average force on sphere B cannot be more than the weight of sphere A. Each sphere has mass 28 g. Deduce whether this statement is correct, using the contact time from part (ii).
questions.answer: Incorrect: the average force on B is about 93 N, far more than the weight of A (0.27 N).
steps: Change in momentum of B = m v = 0.028 x 0.46 = 1.3 x 10^-2 N s.
Average force F = change in momentum / contact time = 1.3 x 10^-2 / 1.4 x 10^-4 = 93 N.
Weight of sphere A = m g = 0.028 x 9.81 = 0.27 N.
93 N is much greater than 0.27 N, so the statement is incorrect.

questions.question: Give two reasons why the circuit did not operate as the student intended.
questions.answer: (1) The voltmeter is not connected across the capacitor when the switch is at X, so the p.d. cannot be measured during charging. (2) At Y the capacitor discharges only through the voltmeter and not through the resistor R.
steps: With the switch at X the capacitor is in the loop with the cell and resistor R, but the voltmeter is on the Y branch and is disconnected, so V cannot be measured while the capacitor charges.
With the switch at Y the capacitor is connected across the voltmeter only: R is in the cell branch, so the capacitor discharges through the voltmeter, not through R as intended.

questions.question: The capacitance is 2.2 uF. Using the V against t graph, determine the resistance in the circuit when the switch was at position Y.
questions.answer: R = about 1.1 x 10^7 ohm (11 megohm)
steps: At Y the capacitor discharges through the voltmeter, so R is the resistance of the voltmeter: V = V0 e^(-t/RC).
V0 = 6.2 V at t = 0. The time constant RC is the time for V to fall to V0/e = 6.2/2.72 = 2.3 V, which the graph gives at t = 24 s.
R = (time constant) / C = 24 / (2.2 x 10^-6) = 1.1 x 10^7 ohm.

questions.question: Determine the average current in the circuit between t = 0 s and t = 30 s, for the capacitor of 2.2 uF.
steps: From the graph V = 6.2 V at t = 0 and V = 1.8 V at t = 30 s, so the capacitor p.d. falls by 4.4 V.
Charge that flows: Delta Q = C Delta V = 2.2 x 10^-6 x 4.4 = 9.7 x 10^-6 C.
Average current = Delta Q / Delta t = 9.7 x 10^-6 / 30 = 3.2 x 10^-7 A.

questions.question: Calculate the energy dissipated by the current in the circuit between t = 0 s and t = 30 s.
steps: The energy dissipated equals the energy lost by the capacitor: Delta E = 1/2 C (V0^2 - V^2).
Delta E = 3.9 x 10^-5 J.

questions.question: A cell of p.d. V0, a capacitor, a resistor and a switch are connected, with the capacitor initially uncharged. Explain the variation of the capacitor p.d. V with time shown in the graph, referring to the charge on the capacitor and the current in the circuit.
questions.answer: The capacitor p.d. rises from zero and approaches V0 asymptotically: as charge builds up the current falls, so the rate of charging falls and the gradient decreases to zero.
steps: Initially the capacitor is uncharged, so V = 0 and the whole p.d. V0 appears across the resistor; the current is at its maximum, V0 / R.
Current flows onto the capacitor plates, so the charge Q on the capacitor increases with time.
V = Q / C increases as the charge increases.
As V rises, the p.d. across the resistor (V0 - V) falls, so the current falls.
A smaller current means charge arrives more slowly, so the gradient of the V-t graph decreases from its maximum at t = 0 towards zero.
The capacitor p.d. therefore approaches the cell e.m.f. V0 exponentially, with the time constant RC controlling how fast.

questions.question: A student selects a capacitor (value shown in the diagram) with tolerance of 20 percent. Calculate the maximum energy such a capacitor can store.
steps: The label shows 2200 microfarad and 25 V (the maximum working p.d.).
With a tolerance of +20 percent the largest capacitance is 1.2 x 2200 = 2640 microfarad = 2.64 x 10^-3 F.
Maximum energy E = 1/2 C V^2 = 0.5 x 2.64 x 10^-3 x 25^2 = 0.825 J, about 0.83 J.

questions.question: The student recorded V every 10 s while the capacitor charged through a resistor. Using the graph of V against t, determine a value for the capacitance C.
questions.answer: C = 2.2 x 10^-4 F (220 microfarad)
steps: While charging V = V0(1 - e^(-t/RC)) with V0 = 6.0 V, the cell p.d. in the circuit diagram.
The time constant RC is the time to reach 63 percent of V0: 0.63 x 6.0 = 3.8 V, which the graph gives at t = 37 s.
Check: V = 2.5 V at t = 20 s gives e^(-t/RC) = 0.58, so RC = 37 s.

questions.question: Sketch on the axes how the current I in the circuit varies with time, including the maximum value of current.
questions.answer: An exponential decay starting at the maximum current 3.6 x 10^-5 A (36 microamp) at t = 0 and falling towards zero (1.3 x 10^-5 A at t = 37 s).
steps: At t = 0 the capacitor is uncharged, so the whole 6.0 V is across the 168 kohm resistor: I_max = 6.0 / 168 000 = 3.6 x 10^-5 A.
As the capacitor charges, the p.d. across the resistor falls, so the current falls exponentially, with decreasing gradient, towards zero.
It falls to 37 percent of the maximum (1.3 x 10^-5 A) after one time constant, 37 s.

questions.question: A second 168 kohm resistor is connected in parallel with the first. Explain how the time taken to charge the capacitor changes, without further calculations.
questions.answer: The time decreases: the parallel combination has a lower resistance, so the time constant RC is smaller and the capacitor charges faster.
steps: Resistors in parallel have a combined resistance smaller than either one: 1/R = 1/R1 + 1/R2.
A lower total resistance gives a smaller time constant RC.
A smaller time constant means the capacitor charges to a given p.d. more quickly.
So the time taken to charge the capacitor decreases.

questions.question: A capacitor of capacitance C with p.d. V stores charge Q. It is replaced by two capacitors of capacitance C each, connected in parallel. Select the total charge stored in the parallel circuit.
questions.answer: D: 2Q
steps: Capacitors in parallel add: C + C = 2C, with the same p.d. V across the combination.
Total charge = (2C) V = 2CV = 2Q, since the single capacitor stored Q = CV (option D).

questions.question: Add to the diagram a suitable circuit to measure the current as the capacitor charges through the resistor.
questions.answer: Add a d.c. supply (with a switch) in series with the resistor and capacitor, and connect an ammeter in series in the same loop.
steps: Complete the series loop with a cell or battery (and switch) so that the capacitor charges through the resistor.
Place an ammeter in series in the loop (any position), so that the same charging current passes through it; it must not be in parallel with a component.

questions.question: The resistance is 5.1 kohm. Using the current against time graph, show that the capacitance of the capacitor is about 0.02 F.
questions.answer: C = 0.018 F, about 0.02 F
steps: During charging I = I0 e^(-t/RC), with I0 = 2.4 mA at t = 0. The time constant RC is the time for I to fall to I0/e = 2.4/2.72 = 0.88 mA.
From the graph I = 0.88 mA at t = 91 s, so RC = 91 s.
C = RC / R = 91 / 5100 = 0.018 F, which is about 0.02 F (to 1 s.f.).

questions.question: Calculate the charge on the capacitor when it is fully charged, using capacitance about 0.02 F and the supply p.d. from the graph.
questions.answer: Q = 0.22 C (about 0.2 C)
steps: At t = 0 all the supply p.d. is across the resistor: V0 = I0 R = 2.4 x 10^-3 x 5.1 x 10^3 = 12.2 V (about 12 V).
When fully charged the capacitor p.d. equals the supply p.d., V0 = 12.2 V.
Q = CV0 = 0.018 x 12.2 = 0.22 C (using C = 0.02 F gives 0.24 C). Check: the area under the I-t graph, about I0 x RC = 2.4 x 10^-3 x 91, is 0.22 C.

questions.question: Calculate the energy stored by the capacitor when it is fully charged.
questions.answer: 1.3 J (about 1 J)
steps: Equivalently E = 1/2 C V0^2 = 0.5 x 0.018 x 12.2^2 = 1.3 J (1.5 J if C is rounded to 0.02 F).

questions.question: A capacitor of capacitance C charged to V0 discharges through a resistor of resistance R. After time t the p.d. is V. Select the expression for the time constant.
questions.answer: D: time constant = -t / ln(V / V0)
steps: During discharge V = V0 e^(-t/RC), so V / V0 = e^(-t/RC).
Taking natural logs: ln(V / V0) = -t / RC.
So the time constant RC = -t / ln(V / V0) (option D).

questions.question: Explain how the current in the circuit varies when the switch is connected to position X to charge the capacitor. No calculations are needed.
questions.answer: The current is at its maximum at the instant the switch closes and then falls exponentially to zero as the capacitor charges and its p.d. approaches the supply p.d.
steps: At the instant the switch is closed the capacitor is uncharged, so the full supply p.d. appears across the resistor and the current is at its maximum.
As charge accumulates on the plates, the capacitor p.d. increases and the p.d. across the resistor falls.
The current therefore decreases continuously as the capacitor charges.
Once the capacitor p.d. equals the supply p.d., the current is zero.

questions.question: Sketch a graph of the variation of current in the circuit as the capacitor is charged, including the maximum value of current.
questions.answer: An exponential decay of current from the maximum 6.4 x 10^-5 A (64 microamp) at t = 0 towards zero, falling to 2.4 x 10^-5 A at t = 59 s.
steps: At t = 0 the capacitor is uncharged, so the 8.0 V is entirely across the 125 kohm resistor: I_max = 8.0 / 125 000 = 6.4 x 10^-5 A.
As the capacitor charges, its p.d. rises, the p.d. across the resistor falls, and the current falls exponentially with decreasing gradient towards zero.
The time constant is RC = 125 000 x 470 x 10^-6 = 59 s, so the current is 37 percent of its maximum (2.4 x 10^-5 A) after 59 s.

questions.question: Show that the time constant of the discharge circuit is about 60 s.
questions.answer: Time constant = RC = 59 s, which is about 60 s.
steps: In position Y the capacitor discharges through the 125 kohm resistor in the lower branch.
RC = 125 x 10^3 x 470 x 10^-6 = 58.75 s, which is about 60 s.

questions.question: The switch is connected to position Y for 3 minutes. Using a time constant of 60 s, determine the percentage of the original p.d. remaining across the capacitor.
questions.answer: About 5.0 percent of the original p.d. remains (e^-3 = 0.050).
steps: Time t = 3 minutes = 180 s.
e^(-3) = 0.0498, so the p.d. remaining is about 5.0 percent of the original.

questions.question: The data logger output shows VC and VR against time during recharging. Determine the p.d. and the time at which the two lines intersect.
questions.answer: p.d. = 4.0 V; time = about 41 s
steps: The cell p.d. is shared between capacitor and resistor at every instant: V_C + V_R = 8.0 V (ammeter and cell resistance negligible).
Where the lines intersect V_C = V_R, so each is 8.0 / 2 = 4.0 V.

questions.question: A second identical capacitor is connected in series with the first, and both are charged through switch position X. Explain how the charge on each capacitor compares with the charge on the single capacitor.
questions.answer: Each capacitor stores half the charge that the single capacitor stores, because the series combination has half the capacitance.
steps: In series the same charge flows onto each capacitor, and the total capacitance is C/2.
The charge on the combination is Q = (C/2) V0, which is half the charge CV0 on the single capacitor.
Each capacitor in the series pair therefore carries half the charge of the single capacitor.

questions.question: Capacitor C1 has half the capacitance of C2 and is charged to half the p.d. of C2. Select the ratio of the energy stored in C1 to that in C2.
steps: Energy stored W = 1/2 C V^2.

questions.topic: Capacitor P.D. At End Of Discharge
questions.question: State the p.d. across the capacitor at the end of a period of discharge, using the graph of the modified output.
questions.answer: About 3.5 V
steps: Each discharge stops where the falling bold line meets the rising original output, at the lowest point of the bold line.
Reading the graph, this lowest p.d. is about 3.5 V (at t of about 2.5 ms, 12.5 ms, 22.5 ms).

questions.question: The capacitor (3.3 uF) discharges through a 6.8 kohm resistor with tolerance 5 percent. Deduce whether the output shown in the graph is consistent with this tolerance.
questions.answer: Consistent: the measured time constant is about 21.6 ms, inside the permitted range 21.3 ms to 23.6 ms (R about 6.5 kohm, 4 percent below 6.8 kohm, within +/-5 percent).
steps: Nominal RC = 6.8 x 10^3 x 3.3 x 10^-6 = 22.4 ms. A tolerance of +/-5 percent gives RC from 21.3 ms to 23.6 ms.
On the graph the capacitor starts to discharge at the peak (t = 5.0 ms, V = 5.0 V) and the discharge ends at about 12.4 ms with V = 3.55 V, a time of 7.4 ms.
This lies within 21.3 to 23.6 ms (R = 21.6 ms / 3.3 microfarad = 6.5 kohm, within 6.46 to 7.14 kohm), so the output is consistent with a +/-5 percent resistor, although near the lower limit.

questions.question: Calculate the change in energy stored in the capacitor during the discharging process shown.
questions.answer: The stored energy decreases by about 2.1 x 10^-5 J
steps: Discharge goes from V1 = 5.0 V (the peak) to V2 = 3.5 V.
Change = 2.1 x 10^-5 J (a decrease).

questions.question: The resistor is replaced by a bulb of much lower resistance than 6.8 kohm. Explain why the output is now very similar to the original output of the power supply.
questions.answer: With a much lower resistance the time constant RC is very short, so the capacitor discharges and recharges quickly and its p.d. follows the supply output closely.
steps: The time constant is RC, so a much lower resistance gives a much smaller time constant.
The capacitor now discharges almost immediately after the supply falls, so its p.d. drops with the supply.
It recharges quickly as the supply rises, so the p.d. across the capacitor tracks the supply output.
The smoothing effect is therefore lost and the output resembles the original supply output.

questions.question: A capacitor is charging and a graph of potential difference against charge is shown. Select the expression giving the capacitance: A the area between the line and the p.d. axis; B the area between the line and the charge axis; C the gradient of the line; D the inverse of the gradient of the line.
questions.answer: D: the inverse of the gradient of the line.
steps: Capacitance is C = Q / V, so V = Q / C.
On a V against Q graph the gradient is dV / dQ = 1 / C.
So the capacitance is the inverse of the gradient, option D.
